sections.html:
Everything runs through the courthouse, 102 E Broadway, Bolivar, MO 65613. The Collector is in Suite 6, (417) 326-4032. The Assessor is in Room 9, with the appraiser line at (417) 326-4346 and personal property at (417) 326-4643. The County Clerk is in Suite 11, (417) 326-4031.

Weekday hours are posted as 8 to 4, though one line shows 8 to 5, so call before a long drive. The collector's office handles more than $24 million a year for schools, roads, general revenue and other districts.

Polk County sits in southwest Missouri, in the Springfield metro area, with Bolivar as the county seat. The assessor counts over 18,000 parcels of real estate. Population is 33,604 across 13,760 housing units, and 71.6 percent of occupied homes are owner-lived. The middle owned home is worth $205,800. The county issued 61 building permits in 2025, so new construction adds a little supply each year but not much.

sections.h2: Tax statements and the penalty date
sections.html:
Bills are typically mailed in early November. When a bill goes missing, ask the collector for a copy. The tax is owed either way. A payment postmarked after December 31 draws a penalty.

The office takes no partial payments and will not accept an incorrect amount. You can pay the personal property bill and the real estate bill on different days. Back taxes from earlier years, though, have to be settled first. Online payment runs through a link on the collector's page, where you can also look up paid status for real and personal accounts.

sections.h2: Who pays when a house is sold
sections.html:
The owner of record is responsible for all taxes due on real property, and Missouri law makes no provision for pro-rating a tax bill. So the split between buyer and seller is worked out by the closing agent on the settlement statement. The county plays no part. Personal property follows ownership on January 1. A truck you sell in March still lands on that year's statement.

Owners are also expected to check that the parcel is described correctly and to give the assessor an updated mailing address. The collector cannot change a valuation without the assessor.

Values are set as of January 1. Full reassessment of real property comes in odd-numbered years, while new construction is added annually. Assessment ratios run 19 percent of market value on residential land and homes, 32 percent on commercial and other, and 12 percent on agricultural. Cars, trucks, boats and campers are assessed at 33.33 percent, farm equipment and livestock at 12 percent, and historic vehicles at 5 percent.

Notices of increased value are mailed in the first week of June, which is when to start gathering evidence. Staff do exterior inspections only, carry photo identification and leave a card when nobody is home. They may not go inside a structure without permission. The assessor does not set the levy. Each taxing district, such as schools, fire, roads, cities, ambulance and hospitals, sets its own.

There are three levels, and each has its own date.

Appeal steps in Polk County
LevelActionDeadline
Informal hearingCall (417) 326-4346 and meet an appraiserBefore June 30
Board of EqualizationGet the form from the County ClerkAppeal by the second Monday of July; hearings in the third week of July
State Tax CommissionFile online at stc.mo.govBy August 15, or thirty days after the board rules if that is later

Ask the clerk at (417) 326-4031 how early the completed board form must arrive, since the second Wednesday in July is the date to plan around. Skipping the board bars any later state appeal. Bring photos, a recent sale or an appraisal, because a change requires proof that the county's records are wrong. To pay under protest on a personal property dispute, tell the collector in writing and file with the State Tax Commission before December 31.

The collector conducts the auction at the courthouse, 10:00 a.m., fourth Monday in August. The parcel list is published in the Bolivar newspaper for three consecutive weeks beforehand. Paying everything owed ahead of the auction stops it for that parcel. Opening bids equal the taxes, penalties and sale costs. Bidders attend in person and sign an affidavit that they owe no delinquent Missouri tax. Many sellers never reach this point, because a payment before the sale ends it.

  • The buyer receives a Certificate of Purchase, held for one year or until redeemed.
  • The former owner has one year to buy the property back, paying the certificate amount plus 10 percent annual interest on the tax.
  • Later years' taxes paid by the buyer carry 8 percent annual interest.
  • Give the collector at least three business days' notice before redeeming, and allow about twenty minutes.

When nobody redeems, the certificate holder can ask for a Collector's Deed, but only after certified-mail notices go out at least ninety days ahead. The certificate becomes void if the requirements are not met by two years after the sale.

If your parcel is on the sale list, call the collector first. Ask for the exact payoff, including penalty, interest and costs, and ask how the office wants the money delivered. A written figure helps, because the closing office will request one. If you plan to list the house instead, tell your agent about the delinquent status early so the payoff is built into the timeline. Earlier delinquent years come before the current one, and a title company will want that whole history cleared before closing.

A traditional listing needs repairs, showings and a buyer's lender, and all of that takes time you may not have before the August sale. A cash sale can close faster, with the back taxes paid from your proceeds at the closing table. If the parcel has already sold at auction, the one-year redemption window is the deadline that matters, and the payoff figure must come from the collector. Take the parcel number and ID to the window, and hold on to each receipt for your closing folder.

The state Property Tax Credit claim, Form 948, is for people who may qualify for a credit or refund. Qualifying seniors and 100 percent disabled individuals can claim up to $750 as renters or $1,100 as owner-occupants, depending on tax or rent paid and household income. For county-level programs beyond that, ask the County Clerk at (417) 326-4031 or the collector at (417) 326-4032.

faqs.q: What is the penalty date for Polk County property tax?
faqs.a: Anything postmarked after December 31 is penalized. Bills normally arrive in early November.

faqs.q: Can I make a partial payment on a Polk County tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The Collector in Bolivar takes no partial payments and will not accept an incorrect amount. Real estate and personal property can be paid on separate days, with older delinquent years first.

faqs.q: When is the Polk County tax sale?
faqs.a: The fourth Monday in August, 10:00 a.m., at the courthouse. Pay the Collector the tax, penalty, interest and costs before then and the parcel comes off the list.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem a Polk County property sold for taxes?
faqs.a: One year from the sale date. Redemption costs the Certificate of Purchase amount plus 10 percent annual interest, plus 8 percent on any later taxes the buyer paid.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Polk County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: Start with the Assessor's appraiser at (417) 326-4346 before June 30, then use the County Clerk's Board of Equalization form. The State Tax Commission comes last, due August 15 or thirty days after the board's decision, whichever falls later.
